bufio.Scanner.summary: bufio.Scanner reads an io.Reader as tokens. By default, each token is one input line without its line ending.
bufio.Scanner.explanation: Scanner reads tokens from an io.Reader. It uses ScanLines by default, so each Scan call returns one line without its line ending. You can choose another split function or provide your own. Use Buffer to allow larger tokens before scanning starts.
bufio.Scanner.syntax:
func NewScanner(r io.Reader) *Scanner
func (s *Scanner) Scan() bool
func (s *Scanner) Bytes() []byte
func (s *Scanner) Text() string
func (s *Scanner) Err() error
func (s *Scanner) Buffer(buf []byte, max int)
func (s *Scanner) Split(split SplitFunc)

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: The input source that provides bytes to scan.

parameters.name: buf, max
parameters.description: A buffer slice used as the initial storage and the maximum buffer size.

parameters.name: split
parameters.description: A function that splits input into tokens.

bufio.Scanner.returns: NewScanner returns *Scanner. Scan returns bool. Err returns error. Bytes returns []byte. Text returns string.

example.title: Read lines from standard input
example.explanation: This reads standard input one line at a time. Scan returns false at the end or after an error. Err reports a non-end-of-file error.

useCases.title: Line input
useCases.scenario: Read a file or standard input one line at a time.

useCases.title: Word input
useCases.scenario: Read space-separated values with bufio.ScanWords.

useCases.title: Custom tokenization
useCases.scenario: Parse a custom token format with a SplitFunc.

interview.question: What does NewScanner do?
interview.answer: NewScanner creates a scanner for an io.Reader and uses ScanLines by default. Each successful Scan makes the current token available through Bytes or Text.
interview.followUp: How can you scan words instead? Set the split function before scanning with scanner.Split(bufio.ScanWords).

interview.question: How do you detect scanner errors?
interview.answer: Scan advances to the next token and returns true when one is available. It returns false at the end of input or after an error, so call Err afterward to check for an actual error.
interview.followUp: What does Err return for io.EOF? It returns nil, because normal end of input is not reported as an error.

interview.question: How do you handle tokens larger than the default limit?
interview.answer: The default maximum token buffer is MaxScanTokenSize, which is 64 KiB. Buffer can set an initial buffer and a larger maximum, but it must be called before scanning starts.
interview.followUp: Why might the real maximum be smaller than the configured value? The buffer can also need space for input such as a newline.

keyPoints: Scanner is a simple choice for reading line-based text.
A split function decides where tokens start and end.
NewScanner uses lines by default and removes the line ending.
Bytes returns the current token without allocating a new string.
Text returns the current token as a newly allocated string.
gotchas: Scanning cannot recover after end of input, the first input error, or a token that exceeds the buffer limit.
Use bufio.Reader when you need detailed error handling, very large tokens, or several sequential scans.
Call Buffer before the first Scan call. Calling it later causes a panic.

bytes.Buffer.summary: bytes.Buffer is a growable byte buffer. Its zero value is ready to use for appending and reading data.
bytes.Buffer.explanation: bytes.Buffer stores bytes that code can append to and read from. Its zero value is ready to use, and reading advances the unread position while writing adds data; Reset keeps its allocated storage for later use.

parameters.name: p
parameters.description: The byte slice to append.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: The number of additional bytes to make room for.

bytes.Buffer.returns: A Buffer holds unread bytes. Read, Next, and ReadByte consume them; Write, WriteString, and WriteRune append data.

example.title: Use a byte buffer
example.explanation: This creates a zero-value buffer, adds text, and prints its unread contents.

useCases.title: Accumulate bytes
useCases.scenario: Build output in pieces before sending or converting it.

useCases.title: Collect reader data
useCases.scenario: Read data from an io.Reader and process it incrementally.

useCases.title: Reuse storage
useCases.scenario: Reuse allocated memory for repeated buffering.

interview.question: What is bytes.Buffer?
interview.answer: A bytes.Buffer is a variable-sized byte buffer. Its zero value is empty and ready for use. Write appends data, while Read consumes unread data.
interview.followUp: What happens when Read has no data? It returns io.EOF, except when the destination slice has length zero.

interview.question: How do Bytes and Len differ?
interview.answer: Bytes returns the unread bytes as a slice, and Len reports their count. The slice aliases the buffer, so later buffer changes can invalidate it.
interview.followUp: How can you preserve the data? Copy the slice into separate storage before modifying the buffer.

interview.question: What does WriteTo do?
interview.answer: WriteTo sends the unread contents to an io.Writer until the buffer is empty or a write fails. It returns the number of bytes written and any error.
interview.followUp: What if the writer accepts fewer bytes without an error? WriteTo returns io.ErrShortWrite.

keyPoints: You can declare a Buffer without initialization.
Next returns and consumes bytes without copying them.
ReadFrom copies from an io.Reader until it reaches EOF.
gotchas: Do not copy a buffer after it has been used. Use a pointer and keep one owner for mutation.
Bytes returns an aliased slice. Do not keep or change it after another buffer operation.
Grow accepts only a non-negative size. A negative value causes a panic.

cap.summary: cap returns a value's capacity. Its meaning depends on the type: it is the reslicing limit for a slice, the element count for an array, or the buffer size for a channel.
cap.explanation: cap reports how far a value can grow or how much storage it has, depending on its type. For a slice, it returns the largest length possible by reslicing. For an array or pointer to an array, it returns the number of elements. For a channel, it returns the buffer capacity. A nil slice or channel has capacity zero.

parameters.name: v
parameters.description: The value whose capacity is measured. It must be an array, pointer to an array, slice, or channel.

cap.returns: An int containing the capacity of v.

example.title: Read a slice's capacity
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    values := make([]int, 2, 5)
    fmt.Println(len(values))
    fmt.Println(cap(values))
}
example.explanation: This creates a slice with length 2 and capacity 5, then prints both values.

useCases.title: Inspect slice storage
useCases.scenario: Check how much a slice can grow before it may need a new underlying array.

useCases.title: Inspect channel buffering
useCases.scenario: Check how many elements a channel buffer can hold.

interview.question: What does cap do?
interview.answer: cap returns capacity according to the argument's type. For a slice, it is the maximum length reachable by reslicing; for an array or pointer to an array, it is the element count; for a channel, it is the buffer capacity.
interview.followUp: What does cap return for a nil slice? It returns zero.

interview.question: How is slice capacity different from slice length?
interview.answer: A slice's capacity is the largest length the slice can reach by reslicing. It can be larger than the current length because the slice may use unused space in its underlying array.
interview.followUp: How can you create a slice with extra capacity? Use make with a third argument, such as make([]int, 0, 10).

interview.question: What does cap return for a channel?
interview.answer: For a channel, cap reports the number of elements its buffer can hold. An unbuffered channel has capacity zero.
interview.followUp: What happens when the channel argument is nil? cap also returns zero.

keyPoints: For a slice, cap is the maximum length reachable by reslicing it.
For an array, cap equals the number of elements, which is also its length.
For a pointer to an array, cap counts the elements in the pointed-to array.
For a channel, cap is the buffer size measured in elements.
gotchas: A nil slice or channel has capacity zero.
For some simple array expressions, the compiler can treat the result as a constant.

Channels.sourceTitle: Effective Go - The Go Programming Language
Channels.summary: Channels let goroutines exchange values and synchronize their work. They may be unbuffered or buffered, and buffered channels can limit concurrent work.
Channels.explanation: Channels let goroutines exchange values and coordinate their progress. An unbuffered channel also synchronizes the sender and receiver; a buffered channel can hold values until a receiver is ready.

parameters.name: T
parameters.description: The element type carried by the channel.

parameters.name: capacity
parameters.description: Optional maximum number of values stored without a receiver.

Channels.returns: `make(chan T)` returns a channel of type `chan T`; it does not return a pointer.

example.title: Send work to a goroutine
example.explanation: A goroutine reads jobs from a channel. Closing the channel ends the range loop. The done channel lets main wait until the worker finishes.

useCases.title: Work distribution
useCases.scenario: Send work to a fixed set of worker goroutines.

useCases.title: Completion signals
useCases.scenario: Tell a caller that an asynchronous operation has finished.

useCases.title: Concurrency limits
useCases.scenario: Restrict how many operations run at the same time.

useCases.title: Parallel request handling
useCases.scenario: Send each request's result back through a channel stored in the request.

interview.question: What is the difference between buffered and unbuffered channels?
interview.answer: An unbuffered channel has no storage for pending values, so sending waits until a receiver takes the value. A buffered channel stores values up to its capacity; sending waits only when that buffer is full.
interview.followUp: How can a buffered channel limit concurrency? Use it as a semaphore: acquire a slot by sending into it, then release the slot by receiving after the work completes.

interview.question: How do you start a goroutine and wait for it?
interview.answer: Prefix a function or method call with `go` to run it in a new goroutine. The caller continues without waiting for that call to finish.
interview.followUp: How can the caller know that the goroutine finished? Have the goroutine send a signal on a channel, then receive that signal in the caller.

interview.question: When should you use a channel instead of a mutex?
interview.answer: Channels are useful for passing ownership, distributing work, and returning asynchronous results. A mutex is often clearer for protecting shared state or implementing a cache.
interview.followUp: What should you do when mutex locking rules become difficult to understand? Consider redesigning the ownership or communication flow with channels if that makes the program simpler.

keyPoints: A goroutine runs a function concurrently with other goroutines and shares the process address space.
Start a goroutine by placing `go` before a function or method call.
Create a channel with `make`; the channel value refers to its underlying communication structure.
Without a capacity argument, `make(chan T)` creates an unbuffered channel.
A buffered channel can act as a semaphore that limits how much work runs at once.
gotchas: Starting a goroutine for every request does not by itself limit concurrent work. Use a fixed worker count when the number of simultaneous calls must be bounded.
A server that only starts workers can keep running forever. Give it a shutdown signal and wait for that signal when it must stop.

close.summary: close shuts down a bidirectional or send-only channel. Receivers can finish queued values, then receive the element type's zero value without blocking; the two-result form reports false.
close.explanation: close stops future sends on a channel. After all queued values are received, receives finish immediately; an empty closed channel returns its element type's zero value and reports false in the two-result form.

parameters.name: c
parameters.description: A bidirectional or send-only channel to close.

example.title: Receive from a closed channel
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan int, 1)
	ch <- 42
	close(ch)

	value, ok := <-ch
	fmt.Println(value, ok)
	value, ok = <-ch
	fmt.Println(value, ok)
}
example.explanation: The first receive gets the sent value. The second receive gets the element type's zero value and reports false because the channel is closed.

useCases.title: Signal producer completion
useCases.scenario: A producer has finished sending all values and needs to signal consumers that no more values will arrive.

useCases.title: Finish a work stream
useCases.scenario: A consumer ranges over a channel and needs the channel to become finished after queued work is processed.

interview.question: What does close do?
interview.answer: close marks a channel so that no more values can be sent. Receives can still obtain values that were sent before the close; after the channel is empty, receives return the element type's zero value without blocking.
interview.followUp: What does the two-result receive return from an empty closed channel? It returns the zero value and sets ok to false.

interview.question: Which channel directions can close accept?
interview.answer: The argument must be a bidirectional channel or a send-only channel. A receive-only channel is not valid because the close operation is performed by the sender.
interview.followUp: Why is a send-only channel allowed? Its direction permits sending, and closing is an operation for the sending side.

interview.question: How can a receiver detect that a channel is closed?
interview.answer: A receive from a closed channel does not block once all previously sent values have been received. In x, ok := <-c, ok is false when c is closed and empty.
interview.followUp: How can code distinguish a real zero value from the end of the channel? Use the two-result receive and check ok rather than checking the received value.

keyPoints: The built-in function closes the supplied channel.
Values sent before closing remain available until receivers consume them.
Once a closed channel is empty, receiving from it completes immediately.
An empty closed channel produces the zero value for its element type.
The two-result receive form reports closure with ok set to false.
gotchas: Close a channel from the sending side, not from the receiving side.
The channel passed to close cannot be receive-only.
Closing does not discard values already sent. Receivers can still read queued values.

context.Context.sourceTitle: Canceling in-progress operations - The Go Programming Language
context.Context.summary: Use context.Context to carry cancellation and deadlines through Go calls. Create a derived context with a timeout, pass it to the operation, and always call the returned cancel function.
context.Context.explanation: A Context carries a deadline, cancellation signal, and request-scoped values across function calls. Derived contexts can be canceled by their own cancel function, by a parent, or by a deadline; code should pass the context explicitly and release resources with cancel.
context.Context.syntax: func WithTimeout(parent Context, timeout time.Duration) (Context, CancelFunc)

parameters.name: parent
parameters.description: The parent context from which the timeout context is derived.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: The maximum duration before the child context is canceled.

context.Context.returns: A derived Context and a CancelFunc. The context is canceled when the timeout expires, the parent is canceled, or cancel is called.

example.title: Stop work after a timeout
example.explanation: This program creates a context with a short timeout. The select stops waiting when the context is canceled.

useCases.title: Bound database work
useCases.scenario: Stop a database query that runs longer than an allowed duration.

useCases.title: Propagate request cancellation
useCases.scenario: Stop server-side work when a client disconnects or cancels a request.

useCases.title: Coordinate goroutines
useCases.scenario: Let a long-running operation stop early when its caller no longer needs the result.

interview.question: What problem does context.Context solve?
interview.answer: A Context carries deadlines, cancellation signals, and request-scoped values. It is passed through function calls so work can stop when the request is canceled or its deadline ends.
interview.followUp: How should a function receive it? Use Context as the first parameter, commonly named ctx, rather than storing it in a struct.

interview.question: How do you add a timeout?
interview.answer: WithTimeout creates a child context whose Done channel closes when the timeout ends, the parent is canceled, or the returned cancel function is called. The caller should call cancel to release resources.
interview.followUp: What error should work usually return after Done closes? Check ctx.Err(), which reports context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded.

interview.question: How does cancellation propagate?
interview.answer: Canceling a parent cancels all contexts derived from it. A CancelFunc tells work to stop but does not wait for that work to finish, and repeated calls after the first have no effect.
interview.followUp: How can cleanup run automatically on cancellation? Use AfterFunc; its callback runs in its own goroutine, and its stop function does not wait for the callback.

keyPoints: The same context can be safely used by several goroutines at the same time.
Err is nil before cancellation and later reports why the context ended.
Use TODO temporarily when a function does not yet have the right context.
gotchas: Use context.TODO when the correct context is not yet known.
Do not use context values for optional function parameters.

context.WithTimeout.summary: context.WithTimeout creates a context that is canceled after a time limit. It returns the new context and a function that can cancel it earlier.
context.WithTimeout.explanation: context.WithTimeout returns a child context with a deadline based on the current time plus the given duration. Its Done channel closes when the timeout expires, the parent is canceled, or the returned cancel function is called. Call cancel when the work finishes to release timer resources.
context.WithTimeout.syntax: func WithTimeout(parent Context, timeout time.Duration) (Context, CancelFunc)

parameters.name: parent
parameters.description: The parent context from which the new context is derived.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: The maximum duration before the returned context is canceled.

context.WithTimeout.returns: A derived Context and a CancelFunc.

example.title: Create a timeout context
example.code:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 100*time.Millisecond)
defer cancel()

select {
case <-time.After(200 * time.Millisecond):
	fmt.Println("overslept")
case <-ctx.Done():
	fmt.Println(ctx.Err())
}
example.explanation: This creates a context that is canceled after 100 milliseconds, then waits for either the timeout or a longer timer.

useCases.title: Limit operation time
useCases.scenario: Stop a slow operation after a fixed duration.

useCases.title: Control request work
useCases.scenario: Pass a cancellation signal through a chain of function calls.

useCases.title: Handle timed waits
useCases.scenario: End a wait when a deadline expires.

interview.question: What does context.WithTimeout return?
interview.answer: It returns a derived Context and a CancelFunc. The child is canceled when the timeout expires, the parent is canceled, or cancel is called.
interview.followUp: What should code do with the CancelFunc? Call it when the operation finishes, usually with defer, so the timer resources are released.

interview.question: How is the timeout represented?
interview.answer: The timeout is relative to the current time. Internally, it behaves like WithDeadline with time.Now().Add(timeout).
interview.followUp: What happens if the parent already has an earlier deadline? The child cannot extend it; the earlier parent deadline remains effective.

interview.question: How can a function react to the timeout?
interview.answer: Use the context's Done channel in a select to stop waiting when cancellation occurs, and inspect ctx.Err() to identify the reason.
interview.followUp: Which standard errors indicate cancellation? context.Canceled indicates cancellation, while context.DeadlineExceeded indicates that a deadline passed.

keyPoints: The function makes a deadline by adding the timeout to the current time.
Waiters can detect the timeout through the context's Done channel.
The child also ends if its cancel function is called or its parent is canceled.
Pass a parent context and a time.Duration to create the timeout context.
gotchas: Call the returned cancel function when the operation ends. This releases resources held by the deadline timer.
The timeout is converted into a deadline from the current time. A parent deadline can still end the child earlier.

copy.summary: The append built-in adds elements to a slice and returns the updated slice. Assign the result because append can reuse existing storage or allocate a new backing array.
copy.explanation: append adds elements to the end of a slice. It may reuse the slice's underlying array when capacity is available, or allocate a new array when it is not. Always use the returned slice because its length or storage can change.

parameters.name: slice
parameters.description: The slice that receives the new elements.

parameters.name: elems
parameters.description: The values added to the end of the slice.

example.title: Append values to a slice
example.code:
slice := make([]int, 0, 2)
slice = append(slice, 10, 20)
println(len(slice))
example.explanation: This creates a slice, adds two values, and prints its length.

useCases.title: Grow a slice
useCases.scenario: Build a list whose size changes while a program runs.

useCases.title: Combine slices
useCases.scenario: Add every element from one slice to another.

useCases.title: Append string bytes
useCases.scenario: Add values to a byte slice from text.

interview.question: What does append do?
interview.answer: append adds elements to the end of a slice and returns the updated slice. The result must usually be assigned back to the slice variable.
interview.followUp: What happens when capacity is too small? A new underlying array is allocated, and the returned slice refers to it.

interview.question: How do you append another slice?
interview.answer: The first argument is the destination slice. The remaining arguments are the elements to add, and a slice can be expanded with the ... syntax.
interview.followUp: Can a string be appended? Yes, the documented special case permits appending a string to a byte slice.

interview.question: When does append allocate?
interview.answer: If the slice has enough capacity, append reslices it to fit the new elements. Otherwise, it allocates a new underlying array.
interview.followUp: Why can ignoring the return value be wrong? The returned slice may have different storage or length, so the original variable may not represent the updated slice.

keyPoints: append adds one or more elements after the current slice contents.
Enough capacity lets append reuse the existing backing array.
Insufficient capacity causes allocation of a new backing array.
The function result is the slice to use after appending.
gotchas: Store the returned slice. The operation can create a new underlying array.
A string can be appended to a byte slice with the special string form.

defer.summary: defer delays a function or method call until its surrounding function is about to return. Calls run in reverse order, and deferred functions can change named return values or recover a panic.
defer.explanation: A defer statement saves a function call for later. Go runs that call just before the surrounding function returns, including during a panic. Deferred calls run in reverse order, and their arguments are evaluated when the defer statement runs. A deferred function can read or change named return values.

parameters.name: Expression
parameters.description: The function or method call to save. Its function value and arguments are evaluated when the defer statement executes.

defer.returns: A deferred call has no direct return value to the surrounding code; any values it returns are discarded.

example.title: Change a named result
example.explanation: The named result is set to "done" first. The deferred function then changes it before run returns.

useCases.title: Release resources
useCases.scenario: A function opens a file, lock, or other resource.

useCases.title: Run cleanup reliably
useCases.scenario: A function must perform a final action on every return path.

useCases.title: Recover from a panic
useCases.scenario: A boundary function must prevent a panic from escaping.

useCases.title: Update a named result
useCases.scenario: A function needs to adjust a named error result before returning.

interview.question: When does a deferred function run?
interview.answer: defer saves the function value and its arguments when the defer statement executes. Go invokes the saved call just before the surrounding function returns, in last-in, first-out order.
interview.followUp: What happens to a deferred call during a panic? Go runs deferred calls while the panic moves up the current goroutine's stack.

interview.question: How can defer affect returned values?
interview.answer: A deferred function can access named result parameters after a return statement has assigned them. It can therefore change the values that the caller receives.
interview.followUp: Can it change an unnamed return value? No. Only named result parameters are directly available to the deferred function.

interview.question: How do panic and recover work together?
interview.answer: panic stops ordinary execution and runs deferred functions while unwinding the current goroutine. recover can capture the panic value only from a deferred function and then resume normal execution.
interview.followUp: What happens if no deferred function recovers? The panic reaches the top of the goroutine's call stack and the program terminates.

keyPoints: If several calls are deferred, the newest one runs first.
A return assigns result parameters before deferred functions run.
The expression after defer must be a function or method call.
recover lets a program handle a panic instead of letting it terminate the goroutine's execution.
Outside the required panic-and-deferred-function situation, recover returns nil.
gotchas: A nil deferred function does not panic when defer is declared. It panics when Go tries to run the deferred call.
recover only works when called directly inside a deferred function during a panic. Otherwise it returns nil.
Recovering stops the panic only if the deferred recovery function finishes normally without starting another panic.

error.summary: Go errors can wrap other errors to add context while preserving the original cause. Use errors.Is and errors.As to inspect the full error chain.
error.explanation: An error can contain another error. The inner error is exposed through Unwrap. Use errors.Is to find a matching error in the chain and errors.As to find a matching error type. Use %w with fmt.Errorf to wrap an error while adding context.
error.syntax:
func (e *QueryError) Unwrap() error
errors.Is(err, target)
errors.As(err, target)
errors.Unwrap(err)
fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)

parameters.name: err
parameters.description: The error value to inspect.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The target error to compare with.

parameters.name: format and arguments
parameters.description: The format string and values used to create an error; one value for %w must be an error.

error.returns: errors.Is and errors.As return a boolean. errors.Unwrap returns the contained error or nil. fmt.Errorf returns an error.

example.title: Wrap and inspect an error
example.explanation: Use %w when adding context and keeping the original error available for errors.Is or errors.As.

useCases.title: Test a known condition
useCases.scenario: Check for a documented sentinel error through several layers of added context.

useCases.title: Inspect a typed error
useCases.scenario: Retrieve fields from a custom error type returned by a lower-level operation.

useCases.title: Preserve the cause
useCases.scenario: Add operation context without losing programmatic access to the original error.

interview.question: What does errors.Is do?
interview.answer: errors.Is checks whether an error or any error it wraps matches a target. It is useful for sentinel errors, such as a package-level permission or not-found error.
interview.followUp: How can a package expose a stable condition without exposing its internal error? Return an error that wraps a documented sentinel, and tell callers to use errors.Is.

interview.question: What does errors.As do?
interview.answer: errors.As searches the error chain for a value of a requested error type. It stores the matching value in the target supplied by the caller.
interview.followUp: Why is the target sometimes a pointer to a pointer? If the error type itself is a pointer, the target must point to a variable of that pointer type.

interview.question: How do you wrap an error?
interview.answer: The %w verb makes fmt.Errorf return an error with an Unwrap method for its error argument. This keeps the original error available to errors.Is and errors.As while adding text.
interview.followUp: When should %w not be used? Do not use it when exposing the underlying error would commit a package to an implementation detail.

keyPoints: An error that contains another error can implement Unwrap() error to return the inner error.
Repeated unwrapping forms an error chain. Inspection functions can search this chain.
Use errors.Is(err, target) to test a sentinel or another matching error in the chain.
Use errors.As to find a specific error type and receive its value.
Use fmt.Errorf with %w to add context and preserve the wrapped error.
By default, errors.Is considers an error a match when it equals the target.
gotchas: Wrapping exposes the inner error to callers, so it becomes part of the package API. Do this only when callers should depend on it.

errors.As.sourceTitle: Working with Errors in Go 1.13 - The Go Programming Language
errors.As.summary: errors.As checks whether an error or one of its wrapped errors has a requested type. It stores the matching error in a target variable when it finds one.
errors.As.explanation: errors.As checks whether an error or any error it wraps has a requested type. Pass a pointer to a variable of that error type. When it finds a match, it stores the matching error in that variable and returns true.
errors.As.syntax: func As(err error, target any) bool

parameters.name: err
parameters.description: The error to inspect. It may contain wrapped errors.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: A pointer to a variable of the desired error type. The variable receives the matching error when found.

errors.As.returns: A bool: true if a matching error is found; otherwise false.

example.title: Check a wrapped error
example.explanation: This program wraps a sentinel error with extra text, then finds it through the error chain.

useCases.title: Find a typed error through wrapping
useCases.scenario: A function may add context with fmt.Errorf and %w before returning an error.

useCases.title: Read fields from a custom error
useCases.scenario: A package returns errors with extra fields, such as a query name or file path.

interview.question: What does errors.As do?
interview.answer: errors.As checks the error itself and each error in its unwrap chain. It returns true when a matching type is found and assigns that error to the target variable.
interview.followUp: How do you use it for an interface? Pass a pointer to a variable whose type is that interface, then test the returned boolean.

interview.question: How is the target argument used?
interview.answer: Declare a variable with the wanted error type, then pass its address to errors.As. For a pointer error type such as *QueryError, the target is **QueryError.
interview.followUp: Why is the extra pointer needed? It lets errors.As write the matched error value into the target variable.

interview.question: Why prefer errors.As over a type assertion?
interview.answer: Use errors.As when wrapping may occur and the caller needs a specific error type. A direct type assertion checks only the outer error, while errors.As examines the whole chain.
interview.followUp: How can a custom error participate in this chain? Give it an Unwrap method that returns its contained error.

keyPoints: It reports whether an error has a requested type.

interview.question: What does errors.New do?
interview.answer: errors.New takes a string and returns an error containing that text. The returned error formats as the supplied text.
interview.followUp: How can callers identify a particular error? Define a shared sentinel error and use errors.Is when wrapped errors may occur.

interview.question: Are two errors.New calls with the same text equal?
interview.answer: Every call to errors.New creates a different error value, even if both calls use identical text. Matching by message is therefore not the same as matching the error value.
interview.followUp: Why is a sentinel useful? Reusing the same declared error lets errors.Is recognize it reliably.

interview.question: How should callers test an error?
interview.answer: Use errors.Is to inspect an error and its wrapped errors for a match. This is preferred to direct equality because wrapping can preserve the underlying error.
interview.followUp: How are multiple wrapped errors handled? errors.Join creates an error with an Unwrap() []error method, and errors.Is can inspect its members.

Identical messages do not make separately created errors the same value.

Use errors.Is rather than direct equality when an error might be wrapped.

An error that unwraps multiple errors must not include nil elements.

parameters.description: A format string containing text and formatting verbs such as %v or %w.

parameters.description: Values used by the format verbs. A %w operand must be an error to wrap it.

useCases.scenario: Preserve several related errors when one operation reports more than one failure.

interview.question: What does fmt.Errorf do?
interview.answer: fmt.Errorf formats the supplied arguments using the format string and returns an error. A %w verb wraps an error operand, preserving it for errors.Unwrap, errors.Is, and errors.As.
interview.followUp: What happens with several %w verbs? The result can unwrap to multiple errors, in the order of the operands in the format arguments.

interview.question: When should %w replace %v or %s?
interview.answer: Use %w when callers need to test or retrieve the underlying error. Use %v or %s when the underlying error should appear only as text and should not be exposed through error unwrapping.
interview.followUp: Why might exposing an underlying error be a problem? Callers may depend on its type or value, making later implementation changes incompatible.

interview.question: How does fmt.Errorf handle multiple wrapped errors?
interview.answer: A single %w creates an error that unwraps to that error. With several valid %w operands, the result provides an Unwrap method returning a slice of the wrapped errors; non-error or nil operands are not included in that slice.
interview.followUp: Does argument order always determine the displayed order? No. Positional format indexes can change display order, while the wrapped-error slice follows the operand order.

keyPoints: Its signature takes a format string followed by zero or more values, and it returns an error.
A wrapped error can be inspected through errors.Unwrap, errors.Is, or errors.As.
More than one %w can preserve several errors in one formatted error.
For multiple wrapped errors, unwrapping returns the valid errors as a slice.
A nil %w operand appears as formatting error text and is not retained in the unwrapped-error slice.
gotchas: Use %w only when callers should be able to inspect the underlying error. Wrapping can expose an implementation detail and limit future changes.

interview.question: What does fmt.Println do?
interview.answer: fmt.Println takes any number of arguments. It formats them using their default formats, separates them with spaces, writes to standard output, and appends a newline.
interview.followUp: How would you write to another destination? Use fmt.Fprintln and pass an io.Writer as the first argument.

interview.question: How is Println different from Print and Printf?
interview.answer: Println uses default formatting, such as decimal output for integers. Unlike Print, it always inserts spaces between arguments and always adds a newline.
interview.followUp: How can you control the exact layout? Use fmt.Printf with a format string and verbs such as %d or %s.

interview.question: What are Println's parameters and return values?
interview.answer: Its signature is func Println(a ...any) (n int, err error). The variadic parameter lets the caller provide any number of values of any type.
interview.followUp: What does the returned byte count represent? It is the number of bytes written to standard output by the underlying writer.

The output has one space between each pair of arguments, followed by one newline.
The variadic parameter accepts zero or more arguments, and each argument can have any type.
Println is implemented by calling Fprintln with os.Stdout, so it uses the standard output writer.
Compared with Print, Println adds spaces without checking whether neighboring operands are strings.
gotchas: Println always inserts spaces, even when an argument is a string. It also always ends the output with a newline.
The returned error should be checked when output errors matter; ignoring it is only suitable when the program does not need to handle such failures.

interview.question: What does fmt.Sprintf do?
interview.answer: fmt.Sprintf formats values according to a format string and returns the resulting string. It does not write to standard output.
interview.followUp: How can the same argument be formatted twice? Use an explicit index such as %[1]v to select the first argument again.

interview.question: How do format verbs work?
interview.answer: A verb controls the representation of an argument. For example, %d formats an integer in base 10, while %s formats a string.
interview.followUp: What happens if the verb and value type do not match? The returned string includes a %! diagnostic describing the mismatch.

interview.question: How are explicit argument indexes used?
interview.answer: The format string can use [n] before a verb to choose the nth one-indexed argument. After that, later verbs normally continue with the following argument unless another index is given.
interview.followUp: Can an index select width or precision? Yes. It can appear before * for a width or precision argument.

%v uses the value's default representation.
%T prints the Go type rather than the value.
%% produces a percent sign and does not consume an argument.
gotchas: Argument indexes start at one, not zero. An index also changes which argument later verbs use.

interview.answer: Stringer generates a self-contained Go source file that adds a String method for a named signed or unsigned integer type. This method makes values satisfy fmt.Stringer.
interview.followUp: What happens for an unknown value? The documentation does not specify the generated behavior for values that do not match a declared constant.

interview.answer: Use the -type flag with a comma-separated list of type names, such as stringer -type=Pill. Without arguments, it processes the package in the current directory.

If names share a value, the alphabetically first matching name is returned.
With -linecomment, a line comment replaces the constant name in the generated text.

Generics.explanation: A generic function declares type parameters in square brackets. Each parameter has a constraint that limits the types callers may provide. The function body must use only operations supported by those constraints. Go can often infer the type arguments from ordinary function arguments, so callers may omit them.

parameters.description: Map key type. It must be comparable because map keys require comparability.

parameters.description: Map value type. It must be either int64 or float64 in the tutorial's constraint.

parameters.description: Map whose values are summed.

interview.question: What are generics in Go?
interview.answer: Generics let functions and types work with a permitted set of types. A generic declaration has type parameters in square brackets, and each parameter has a constraint.
interview.followUp: What are the three main additions described for generics? Type parameters, interfaces that define sets of types, and type inference.

interview.question: What is a type constraint?
interview.answer: A constraint limits the types that can be used for a type parameter. It also determines which operations are valid in the generic function body.
interview.followUp: Why does `V` need a numeric constraint in a sum function? The body uses `+=`, so the constraint must permit numeric values.

interview.question: How does type inference work with generic functions?
interview.answer: Go can infer type arguments from the ordinary arguments passed to a generic function. Therefore, a call often does not need explicit type arguments in square brackets.
interview.followUp: When would explicit type arguments still be useful? They can make the selected types clear or help when inference cannot determine them.

keyPoints: Generic functions and types can be written once for a defined set of types.
Type parameters appear in square brackets before ordinary function parameters.
Each type parameter has a constraint that states which type arguments are allowed.
During compilation, a type parameter represents the one concrete type selected by the caller.
Calls can omit type arguments when Go can derive them from ordinary arguments.
gotchas: A constraint must allow every operation used on its type parameter. Otherwise, the generic function does not compile.

interview.question: What does go fmt do?
interview.answer: go fmt formats the source files in the named Go packages. Internally, it runs gofmt with list and write options, then reports modified files.
interview.followUp: How would you format one file with custom gofmt options? Run gofmt directly instead of using go fmt.

interview.question: What are the -n and -x flags?
interview.answer: The -n flag prints the commands that would run without executing them. The -x flag prints commands as they execute.
interview.followUp: Why might -n be useful? It lets you inspect the planned formatting commands before changing files.

interview.question: How does go generate choose and order commands?
interview.answer: It scans files for lines beginning exactly with //go:generate. It runs the commands in package order, then file-name order, then source order within each file.
interview.followUp: What happens after a generator fails? The remaining generators for that package are skipped, while processing of other packages follows the command-line package order.

interview.question: What do the main go generate flags do?
interview.answer: The command supports -run with a regular expression that selects directives by their complete original directive text, excluding trailing spaces and the final newline. The -n flag prints commands without running them, and -x prints commands as they run.
interview.followUp: Does -run match only the generator name? No. It matches the full original source text of the directive.

interview.question: Which environment variables can a generator use?
interview.answer: Generators receive variables such as GOARCH, GOOS, GOFILE, GOLINE, and GOPACKAGE. The command also provides GOROOT, PATH, and DOLLAR; PATH starts with the Go toolchain's bin directory.

A failed generator stops later generators for the same package.

interview.answer: It creates a go.mod file and sets the module path. The file also records the Go version and later lists dependency requirements.
interview.followUp: Why does the module path matter? It identifies the module and is the import prefix for its packages.

interview.question: How should you choose a module path?
interview.answer: The module path usually names the repository location from which Go tools can download the module. It must be usable as a download location if the module will be published.
interview.followUp: What changes for a v2 module? Its module path must end with /v2, such as example.com/mymodule/v2.

interview.question: What information belongs in go.mod?
interview.answer: The go.mod file describes the module's path, minimum Go version, required module versions, and optional replacement or exclusion rules. Go commands help keep these requirements consistent.
interview.followUp: Which commands can manage the file? go get, go mod tidy, and go mod edit can manage dependencies and edit the requirements.

keyPoints: Running go mod init creates the module's go.mod file.
The module path is also the import prefix for every package in the module.
Dependency versions in go.mod help make builds reproducible and controllable.
Use Go commands to maintain dependency requirements and the go.mod file.
gotchas: For a v2 or later module, include the major version suffix in the module path, such as /v2.
The go directive sets the minimum Go version required by the module. Newer declared versions can prevent older toolchains from using it.

interview.question: What does go mod tidy do?
interview.answer: go mod tidy makes go.mod match the packages imported by the main module and its tests. It adds missing module requirements and removes unused ones.
interview.followUp: How does it handle indirect dependencies?

interview.question: What files can go mod tidy change?
interview.answer: It updates go.sum with checksums needed for dependency modules. It also formats go.mod in the standard form.
interview.followUp: Why can go.sum contain checksums for versions not used directly?

interview.question: How should dependency changes be checked?
interview.answer: Run it from the module root, then run go build ./... and go test ./.... Review the selected modules with go list -m all when migrating or changing dependencies.
interview.followUp: How can you investigate an unexpected selected version?

Missing providers lead to new requirements in go.mod.
The command records dependency checksums in go.sum for the Go version rules described by the module.
It normalizes go.mod formatting so later automatic edits create smaller diffs.

Tests that write beside package files can fail because cached module directories are read-only. Use a temporary directory instead.

interview.question: What does `go run` do?
interview.answer: `go run` compiles and runs a named main package. It is useful during development, but it does not install the program as a reusable executable.
interview.followUp: How can you run a package without changing the current module's dependencies? Use a package argument with a version suffix, such as `@latest`.

interview.question: Which package forms can `go run` accept?
interview.answer: The package can be a list of Go files from one directory, an import path, a file-system path, or a pattern for one known package. The common current-directory form is `go run .`.
interview.followUp: What does `go run .` depend on? It uses the current module context when module-aware mode is enabled.

interview.question: How does `-exec` change `go run`?
interview.answer: Without `-exec`, Go normally runs the compiled binary directly. With `-exec`, Go invokes that binary through the named program.
interview.followUp: When can Go use a target-specific executor automatically? For a different `GOOS` or `GOARCH`, it can use a matching `go_$GOOS_$GOARCH_exec` program on the search path.

keyPoints: The command compiles and runs the selected main package.
A package is commonly selected with Go files from one directory.
Import paths, file-system paths, and single-package patterns are also supported.

interview.answer: Name the file with the _test.go suffix. Put a function such as TestHello(t *testing.T) in it. Run go test to execute the test.
interview.followUp: How can you show output from successful tests? Use go test -v, which prints every test and logging output.

interview.question: How does a test report failure?
interview.answer: A test receives *testing.T. Calling methods such as t.Errorf reports a failure while preserving formatted diagnostic values.
interview.followUp: How can you run only selected tests? Use go test -run with a regular expression matching the test name.

interview.question: What does go test do in different invocation modes?
interview.answer: With no package argument, go test tests the package in the current directory and prints a final status with elapsed time. With package arguments, it tests each listed package and shows detailed output for failures.

interview.question: What is `go vet` used for?
interview.answer: Use `go vet` to find suspicious source-code patterns that compilers might miss. A common example is a `Printf` call whose arguments do not match its format string.
interview.followUp: What does a nonzero status mean? It means the invocation was invalid or a problem was reported.

interview.question: How do you choose packages for vetting?
interview.answer: `go vet` checks the package in the current directory. A pattern such as `./...` selects packages recursively according to Go package-pattern rules.
interview.followUp: How can you learn more package patterns? Run `go help packages`.

interview.question: How are vet checks selected?
interview.answer: The tool supports checks including `printf`, `copylocks`, `atomic`, `buildtag`, and `errorsas`. By default, all checks run unless explicit check flags change the selection.
interview.followUp: What does `-printf=false` do? It runs all checks except the `printf` check.

It can identify some problems that compilation does not catch.
A package path or pattern can select the packages to check.

interview.question: What is a goroutine?
interview.answer: A goroutine is a function running concurrently with other functions in the same address space. It starts with a small stack that grows when needed, so many goroutines can use relatively little memory.
interview.followUp: How does Go keep a blocked goroutine from stopping other work? The runtime moves runnable goroutines to another operating-system thread when a goroutine blocks, such as during I/O.

interview.question: How do you start a goroutine and wait for its result?
interview.answer: Prefix a function or method call with the go keyword. The call then runs in a new goroutine, and the caller does not wait for it to finish.
interview.followUp: How can the caller know that work finished? Use a channel or another synchronization mechanism to send and receive a completion signal.

interview.question: Does using goroutines always make a program faster?
interview.answer: Concurrency structures a program as independently executing components. Parallelism runs computations at the same time on multiple CPUs. Goroutines make concurrency easier, but they do not make a sequential problem parallel.
interview.followUp: Why might more CPUs reduce performance? Extra synchronization, communication, and context switching can cost more than the useful computation.

keyPoints: A goroutine runs a function concurrently with other goroutines and shares the program's address space.
Start a goroutine by putting go before a function or method call.
A goroutine ends when its function call returns. It does not automatically report completion.
The runtime schedules goroutines across operating-system threads, allowing other work to continue when one goroutine blocks.
Goroutine stacks begin small and grow or shrink as the function needs more or less space.

GOMAXPROCS limits goroutines that execute at the same time. It does not limit the total number of operating-system threads or blocked goroutines.

interview.question: How should an HTTP response be handled?
interview.answer: A successful call can return a response with a non-nil body even when the status is not in the 2xx range. The caller must close that body after use.
interview.followUp: Why does closing matter? It allows the underlying transport to reuse a persistent TCP connection.

interview.question: What does embedding one interface in another do?
interview.answer: Embedding interfaces creates a new interface whose method set includes the methods of each embedded interface. A value satisfies the new interface only when it satisfies all of those requirements.
interview.followUp: Can an interface embed a struct type? No. Interface embedding is for interfaces; struct embedding is a separate feature.

interview.question: How does struct embedding differ from interface embedding?
interview.answer: A struct can embed fields without field names. Methods of the embedded fields can then be promoted, so callers can use them through the outer struct.
interview.followUp: What must be done when the embedded field is a pointer? Initialize it to a valid object before using the promoted methods.

interview.question: Is Go embedding a form of inheritance?
interview.answer: Embedding does not provide class inheritance or subclassing. It lets a type combine interface requirements or reuse implementation through embedded struct fields.
interview.followUp: How can a type satisfy an interface without explicitly declaring that relationship? By implementing every method required by the interface.

An interface embedding Reader and Writer requires the capabilities of both.
A struct can embed types as unnamed fields.

interview.question: What does ioutil.ReadAll do?
interview.answer: ioutil.ReadAll reads from an io.Reader until EOF or another error. It returns the bytes read and a non-EOF error, if one occurred. In new code, use io.ReadAll.
interview.followUp: How would you protect a service from an untrusted large input? Use io.LimitReader or another size limit before reading all data.

interview.question: How does ReadAll handle EOF and errors?
interview.answer: A successful read returns err == nil. EOF is expected because the function reads until EOF, so EOF is not reported as the error for a successful call.
interview.followUp: What happens if the reader returns data and a real error? The returned bytes can contain data read before the error, and the error is reported.

interview.question: What is the main resource risk of ReadAll?
interview.answer: ReadAll stores the complete input in a byte slice, so memory use grows with the input size. It is suitable only when the complete input can safely fit in memory.

interview.question: What is bytes.Reader?
interview.answer: bytes.Reader reads from a byte slice and keeps a current index. It is read-only, and its zero value behaves like a reader over an empty slice.

interview.question: How does Read behave at the end?
interview.answer: Read returns up to the size of the destination slice and advances the current index. At the end, it returns zero and io.EOF.
interview.followUp: How can you read from a fixed position without changing state? Use ReadAt with a nonnegative offset.

interview.question: How does Seek work?
interview.answer: Seek accepts offsets relative to the start, current position, or end. It rejects an invalid whence and any resulting negative position.
interview.followUp: What happens to rune unread state after seeking? Seek clears the previous-rune state, so UnreadRune cannot undo a prior ReadRune.

interview.question: What does json.Unmarshal do?
interview.answer: json.Unmarshal takes JSON bytes and a destination value. It decodes the bytes and writes the result through the destination pointer. It returns an error if decoding fails.
interview.followUp: What happens if the destination is not a pointer? It returns an InvalidUnmarshalError because the function cannot store the result there.

interview.question: Which Go values can receive an object?
interview.answer: A JSON object can be decoded into a struct or map when the JSON values match the Go field or element types. Struct fields can use json tags to control their JSON names.
interview.followUp: How can a program reject fields it does not recognize? Use Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields when decoding with a Decoder.

interview.question: What types are used for JSON decoded into interface values?
interview.answer: When decoding into interface values, JSON objects become maps, arrays become slices, strings become strings, booleans become bool, numbers become float64, and null becomes nil.
interview.followUp: How can number precision be preserved for interface values? Use Decoder.UseNumber, then interpret the resulting json.Number explicitly.

It parses the input and writes the decoded result into the pointed-to value.
JSON null can produce nil for interfaces, maps, pointers, and slices.
For a non-null JSON value, a nil pointer target is allocated before decoding.
gotchas: A nil value or a non-pointer target causes an InvalidUnmarshalError.
JSON null can set pointer-like values to nil; check whether that is valid for your data.

len.explanation: The len function reports a value's size based on its type. For slices and maps, it counts elements. For strings, it counts bytes. For channels, it counts unread buffered elements. A nil slice, map, or channel has length zero.

parameters.name: v
parameters.description: The value whose length is measured. It can be an array, pointer to an array, slice, map, string, or channel.

len.returns: An int containing the length of the supplied value.

useCases.title: Inspect buffered data
useCases.scenario: Check how many values are waiting in a buffered channel.

interview.question: What does the len built-in function return?
interview.answer: len returns an int. Its meaning depends on the argument: it counts array elements, slice or map entries, string bytes, or unread buffered channel elements.
interview.followUp: What does len return for a nil slice? It returns zero.

interview.question: Does len count characters in a string?
interview.answer: For a string, len returns the number of bytes in the string. It does not directly count Unicode characters.
interview.followUp: How can code count Unicode code points instead? Convert the string to a rune slice and use its length.

interview.question: What does len report for a channel?
interview.answer: A channel's length is the number of values currently queued in its buffer. For a nil channel, len returns zero.
interview.followUp: Does len tell you how many values will ever be received? No. It only reports the current unread buffered count.

keyPoints: For an array, len returns its fixed element count.
A pointer to an array uses the pointed-to array's element count, even when the pointer is nil.
For some constant expressions, the compiler can determine len at compile time.
The language specification describes when len can produce a constant result.
gotchas: len counts bytes in a string, not the number of characters.
For a channel, len reports buffered values that have not been received.
A nil slice or map is safe to pass to len and returns zero.

interview.question: How does make differ from new?
interview.answer: make initializes a slice, map, or channel and returns a value of that type. new allocates a zero-valued variable and returns a pointer to it.
interview.followUp: What does make([]int, 0, 10) create? It creates a zero-length slice with capacity 10 and an underlying array of size 10.

interview.question: What do the size arguments mean for slices and maps?
interview.answer: For a slice, the first size is its length. An optional second size sets capacity and must be at least the length. For a map, the size is an initial space hint.
interview.followUp: Can a map grow past the value passed to make? Yes. The hint does not set a maximum size.

interview.question: How does make initialize a channel?
interview.answer: For a channel, the size sets buffer capacity. With no size or a zero size, the channel is unbuffered; otherwise it is buffered.
interview.followUp: When can an unbuffered channel operation proceed? Sending and receiving succeed only when both a sender and receiver are ready.

The first argument must be a type, such as []int, map[string]int, or chan int.
For slices, the first size argument determines the length.
For maps, make returns an empty initialized map and may reserve space for the requested number of elements.
For channels, the size controls how many values the buffer can hold before sends block.
gotchas: make returns the created value, not a pointer. Do not use it when you need a pointer to a new variable.
A slice's capacity equals its length unless you provide a second capacity argument. That capacity cannot be smaller than the length.
A map capacity is only a starting hint. It does not limit how many entries the map can hold.

func Clone[M ~map[K]V, K comparable, V any](m M) M

func EqualFunc[M1 ~map[K]V1, M2 ~map[K]V2, K comparable, V1, V2 any](m1 M1, m2 M2, eq func(V1, V2) bool) bool

interview.question: How does maps.Equal compare two maps?
interview.answer: Equal first checks the map lengths. It then checks every key in the first map and compares the matching value with ==.
interview.followUp: What if values are not comparable? Use EqualFunc with a comparison function, because Equal requires comparable values.

interview.question: What does maps.Clone copy?
interview.answer: Clone returns a new map with the same keys and values. The operation is shallow, so values are assigned rather than recursively copied.
interview.followUp: What happens when a map value is a slice? The cloned map and original map refer to the same slice, so changing its elements is visible through both maps.

interview.question: What does maps.Copy do when keys overlap?
interview.answer: Copy adds every key and value from src to dst. If a key already exists in dst, the value from src replaces it.
interview.followUp: How can selected entries be removed? Use DeleteFunc and return true from its predicate for entries that should be deleted.

keyPoints: The package uses generic functions, so it works with many named map types.
Equal returns true only when both maps contain matching keys and values.
EqualFunc supports different value types when a supplied function says whether two values match.
Copy changes dst directly; it does not create and return a new map.
DeleteFunc uses a predicate that receives each key and value.
All provides key-value pairs as an iterator.
gotchas: Floating-point NaN keys have no special handling in this package.
Clone is shallow. Reference-like values such as slices remain shared between the original and cloned maps.
Do not rely on the order produced by Keys or Values.

maps.Keys.summary: maps.Keys returns an iterator over a map's keys. The order is unspecified and may differ between calls.
maps.Keys.explanation: maps.Keys returns an iterator over the keys in a map. The order is not specified, so sort the result when stable output is needed.

interview.question: What does maps.Keys return?
interview.answer: maps.Keys takes a map and returns an iter.Seq[K] iterator over its keys. The key type must be comparable because Go map keys must be comparable.
interview.followUp: How can you produce deterministic output? Use slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) to collect and sort the keys.

interview.question: Can maps.Keys preserve map order?
interview.answer: The returned sequence has no defined order. Two calls can produce different orders, so callers should not use the sequence as an ordering guarantee.
interview.followUp: What should code do before displaying keys in tests or user output? Sort them with slices.Sorted.

interview.question: What map types can maps.Keys accept?
interview.answer: The function is generic over map types with the form ~map[K]V. It returns keys of type K and accepts any value type V.
interview.followUp: What happens with an empty map? The iterator contains no keys, so consuming it produces an empty result.

The key order can change between calls.
The function accepts a map with comparable keys and returns iter.Seq[K].
Use slices.Sorted with maps.Keys when you need keys in sorted order.
gotchas: Do not depend on the order of keys returned by maps.Keys.

new.explanation: In Go 1.26, new accepts an expression instead of only a type. It evaluates the expression, stores the result in a newly allocated variable, and returns a pointer to that variable. The expression must produce the value's type, such as int64(300) for a *int64 result.

new.returns: A pointer to a newly allocated variable containing the expression's value.

example.explanation: This creates an int64 value initialized to 300 and returns a pointer to it.

useCases.title: Computed pointer values

interview.question: What changed about new in Go 1.26?
interview.answer: Go 1.26 lets new take an expression, such as new(int64(300)). The expression supplies the initial value, and new returns a pointer to the new variable.
interview.followUp: How would you create a pointer to a computed value? Use an expression of the desired type, such as new(len(items)) for an int value.

interview.question: What does new(int64(300)) return?
interview.answer: new(int64(300)) creates a new int64 variable initialized to 300 and returns *int64. This can make optional pointer fields easier to populate in one expression.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful with JSON? A pointer can distinguish an absent or null optional field from a present field whose value is zero.

interview.question: Give a practical use for the new expression form.
interview.answer: The operand expression determines the initial value. For example, new(yearsSince(born)) creates an initialized pointer that can be assigned to an *int field.
interview.followUp: What must the expression satisfy? Its result must have the type expected by the pointer context, or be assignable to that type.

keyPoints: Use new(expression) when you need a pointer to an already computed value.
The result of new(int64(300)) has type *int64 and points to a value of 300.
This syntax is useful for optional fields represented by pointers.
A struct literal can initialize an optional pointer field without a temporary variable.
gotchas: This form is available in Go 1.26 and later. It is different from the older form, which takes a type and creates its zero value.

interview.question: How does Load behave?
interview.answer: Load reads environment files and does not replace values that already exist. It returns an error when loading fails.
interview.followUp: How do you replace existing values? Use OverLoad for files or OverApply for an io.Reader.

interview.question: When would you use Apply?
interview.answer: Apply accepts an io.Reader, so the source does not need to be a file. It also preserves an existing environment value.
interview.followUp: How would you replace that value? Call OverApply with the reader instead.

interview.question: What does Must do?
interview.answer: Must is a helper for turning a loading error into a panic. It is useful when startup cannot continue without the variables.
interview.followUp: What happens with a missing file? Load returns an error, and Must causes a panic if given that call.

When several files are passed to Load, earlier values take precedence.
Apply can read environment data from strings, files, or other reader sources.
The override functions replace values already present in the environment.

interview.question: What does os.Open do?
interview.answer: os.Open takes a file name and returns (*File, error). It opens the file with read-only access. The caller should check the error and close the file after use.
interview.followUp: How would you open a file for writing instead? Use os.OpenFile with flags such as O_WRONLY and O_CREATE, plus a permission mode.

interview.question: How does File.Read report the amount of data read?
interview.answer: Read copies up to len(b) bytes from the file into b. It returns the number copied and an error. At the end of the file, it returns 0 and io.EOF.
interview.followUp: Why should code use data[:n]? Because n is the number of valid bytes read; the rest of the buffer may not contain file data.

interview.question: Can multiple goroutines use the returned File?
interview.answer: Open returns a *File that represents an open file descriptor. File methods are safe for concurrent use, but the operating system may limit concurrent operations.
interview.followUp: What can happen if the limit is exceeded? Performance may get worse, or other problems may occur.

The buffer length sets the maximum number of bytes read in one call.
Multiple goroutines may use a File's methods safely, subject to operating-system limits.

Opening a missing or inaccessible path returns a *PathError.

os.ReadFile.explanation: os.ReadFile opens the named file, reads all its contents into a byte slice, and returns that slice with an error value. A successful read returns a nil error. The function is useful when the complete file fits in memory.

interview.question: What does os.ReadFile return?
interview.answer: os.ReadFile takes a file name and returns the complete contents as []byte plus an error. The error is nil when the read succeeds.
interview.followUp: What should code do with the returned error? It should check it before using the data, then handle or return the error instead of ignoring it.

interview.question: How does os.ReadFile handle EOF?
interview.answer: It reads the whole named file into memory. It does not return a successful read together with io.EOF.
interview.followUp: When would another API be better? Use an os.File reader or a streaming approach when processing a large file incrementally.

interview.question: What kind of error can a failed read return?
interview.answer: A failed call returns an error of type *os.PathError. This error carries the operation and path, which helps identify the failure.
interview.followUp: How can a caller inspect the underlying cause? Use errors.As to obtain a *os.PathError, then inspect its fields or unwrap its underlying error.

Check whether the error is nil to confirm success. Do not expect io.EOF for a complete read.
Its result types are []byte for the contents and error for the operation result.
The function works well for simple configuration, text, or small data files that need to be loaded at once.

File errors have type *os.PathError. The error includes information about the failed path and operation.

panic.summary: panic starts stack unwinding and runs deferred functions. recover can stop that unwinding only when called directly by a deferred function in the same goroutine.
panic.explanation: panic starts stack unwinding and runs deferred functions. recover can stop that unwinding only when called directly by a deferred function in the same goroutine.

interview.question: What does panic do?
interview.answer: panic stops the current function and starts unwinding the goroutine's stack. Deferred functions run during this unwinding. If no deferred function recovers it, the program exits with a stack trace.
interview.followUp: Can one goroutine recover a panic from another? No. Recovery must happen in the panicking goroutine.

interview.question: Where can recover be used?
interview.answer: recover must be called directly inside a deferred function. It returns the value passed to panic and stops the stack from unwinding when recovery succeeds.
interview.followUp: What happens if recover returns nil? The deferred function did not recover a non-nil panic value, so normal panic handling continues.

interview.question: When should a package use panic?
interview.answer: Use panic inside a package for deeply nested internal failures when an exported function can translate the panic into an error. Do not let an explicit panic cross the package boundary.
interview.followUp: Why use this pattern? It can avoid manually returning an error through every internal call while keeping the public API error-based.

keyPoints: panic begins unwinding the current goroutine's stack, and recover can stop that process.
Deferred functions run while the stack is being unwound.
recover is useful only when called from a deferred function.
A successful recover returns the panic value.
The runtime can panic for failures such as an out-of-bounds array or slice index.
An unrecovered panic at a goroutine's top level ends the program and prints a stack trace.
gotchas: Calling recover outside a deferred function does not stop a panic.
Packages should usually return errors instead of exposing panics to callers.

Slices.explanation: A slice is a small descriptor for part of an underlying array. It has a length and a capacity. Assigning or passing a slice copies the descriptor, so slices can share the same array. Use append to add elements; keep the returned slice because append can create a new array.

interview.question: What is a slice in Go?
interview.answer: A slice contains a pointer to array data, a length, and a capacity. It refers to a range of an underlying array rather than storing all elements itself.
interview.followUp: What happens when a slice is passed to a function? The slice descriptor is copied, but both descriptors can refer to the same array, so element changes can be visible to the caller.

interview.question: How does append work?
interview.answer: append adds elements and returns the resulting slice. If the current capacity is insufficient, it allocates new storage and copies the old elements.
interview.followUp: Why must the result be assigned? The returned descriptor may contain a new pointer, length, or capacity after reallocation.

interview.question: How are slices allocated?
interview.answer: make initializes a slice and creates its backing storage. For example, make([]int, 10, 100) creates length 10 and capacity 100.
interview.followUp: How does make differ from new for slices? make returns an initialized slice, while new returns a pointer to a zeroed slice structure, whose value is nil.

keyPoints: Two slice values can share the same underlying array.
A slice can be resliced to a different length within its capacity.
Use the built-in append function for common slice growth.
Use make when you need an initialized slice ready for use.
A two-dimensional slice is represented as a slice of slices, such as [][]byte.
gotchas: A slice can grow only up to its capacity without replacing its underlying array.
Changing slice elements is visible through shared storage, but changing the slice length is not visible unless the returned slice is used.
For a two-dimensional slice, independently allocated rows are safer when rows can change size.

slices.Sort.explanation: slices.Sort orders a slice whose element type supports Go's ordered comparisons. It changes the original slice. Floating-point NaN values come before other values.

interview.question: What does slices.Sort do?
interview.answer: slices.Sort sorts an ordered slice in ascending order and changes that slice in place. It is not a stable sort.
interview.followUp: What happens with NaN values? They are ordered before other floating-point values.

interview.question: What type can be sorted?
interview.answer: The element type must satisfy cmp.Ordered. This allows the function to use Go's normal ordering for supported numeric and string types.

interview.question: What methods must sort.Interface provide?
interview.answer: Implement Len, Less, and Swap. Len returns the number of elements, Less compares two indexes, and Swap exchanges the elements at those indexes.
interview.followUp: Why use indexes instead of values? The interface can adapt sorting to many collection types while keeping the sorting algorithm independent of the collection's element type.

interview.question: How does Sort differ from Stable?
interview.answer: Sort orders elements according to Less and is not stable. It makes one Len call and uses a number of Less and Swap calls proportional to n log n.
interview.followUp: How do you preserve equal-element order? Call Stable instead; it keeps equal elements in their original input order.

interview.question: What makes a valid Less function?
interview.answer: Less must define a strict weak ordering. In particular, ordering must remain transitive, and pairs that compare equal must behave consistently.
interview.followUp: What special issue occurs with float values? NaN breaks ordinary floating-point ordering, so use the documented NaN-aware comparison used by Float64Slice.

The methods work with integer indexes, so the interface can represent user-defined collections.
Len tells the sorting algorithm how many elements it must process.
Swap gives the algorithm a way to rearrange two positions in the collection.
Sort uses Less as the definition of ascending order rather than assuming a built-in element type.
gotchas: Less must be transitive and consistent. If it violates these rules, sorting behavior is not valid.

interview.question: What does strings.Join do?
interview.answer: strings.Join takes a slice of strings and a separator, then returns one string with the separator between elements. An empty slice returns an empty string, and a one-element slice returns that element unchanged.

interview.answer: The separator is inserted only between elements. For example, joining ["a", "b", "c"] with ":" produces "a:b:c".

interview.question: How does Join handle an output that is too large?
interview.answer: Join checks for output-length overflow before allocating the result. If the required length is too large, it panics with an overflow error.
interview.followUp: Why can the output be larger than the input elements? Each separator adds its length once for every gap between elements.

The separator appears between neighboring elements.
The result starts with the first element.
For each later element, Join writes the separator before writing that element.

sync.Map.explanation: sync.Map is a map for concurrent use by multiple goroutines. It provides operations such as loading, storing, deleting, replacing, and iterating without requiring an additional lock.
