interview.question: What problem does sync.Map solve?
interview.answer: sync.Map supports concurrent access without an extra mutex. Its zero value is ready for use, and its operations provide synchronization between observed writes and reads.
interview.followUp: When might a normal map be better? A normal map with suitable locking usually gives better type safety and makes related invariants easier to maintain.

interview.question: How do Load and LoadOrStore differ?
interview.answer: Load returns the value for a key and an ok result. ok is false when the key is absent, so callers can distinguish a missing entry from a stored nil-like value.
interview.followUp: How can a caller initialize a value only once? Use LoadOrStore, which returns the existing value when present or stores the supplied value otherwise.

interview.question: What guarantees does Range provide?
interview.answer: Range calls a function for each present key and value. Returning false stops the iteration, but concurrent changes can affect which mapping is observed.
interview.followUp: Can the callback use the same Map? Yes. Range does not block other methods, and the callback may call methods on the Map.

Load, Store, and Delete have amortized constant-time behavior.
It is suited to write-once, read-many caches and to disjoint key sets used by multiple goroutines.

sync.Mutex.summary: sync.Mutex provides mutual exclusion: one goroutine can hold the lock at a time. Lock waits for ownership, TryLock attempts without waiting, and Unlock releases the lock.
sync.Mutex.explanation: A Mutex allows only one goroutine at a time to enter a protected section. Lock waits until the mutex can be acquired, while Unlock releases it. The implementation uses a fast atomic path and a waiting path; after long waits it can switch to starvation mode, which hands ownership directly to the next waiter.

interview.question: What is a Mutex?
interview.answer: A Mutex is a mutual exclusion lock. Lock acquires it, and Unlock releases it so another goroutine can enter the protected section.
interview.followUp: What happens when many goroutines wait? The implementation queues them and may enter starvation mode after a wait longer than 1 ms.

interview.question: How does TryLock differ from Lock?
interview.answer: TryLock returns false when the mutex is locked or starving. Otherwise it uses an atomic compare-and-swap to attempt acquisition and returns true only if that attempt succeeds.
interview.followUp: Can TryLock still fail when the mutex appears available? Yes. Another goroutine can change the state before the compare-and-swap succeeds.

interview.question: How does the mutex handle fairness?
interview.answer: In normal mode, a woken waiter competes with newly arriving goroutines. In starvation mode, the unlocking goroutine directly hands ownership to the waiter at the front of the queue.
interview.followUp: When does starvation mode end? A waiter switches back to normal mode if it is the last waiter or waited less than 1 ms.

keyPoints: A Mutex prevents multiple goroutines from holding the same lock at the same time.
The common case uses an atomic operation to acquire an unlocked mutex quickly.
Contended locking uses a separate slow path so the common Lock path can remain efficient.
TryLock makes a non-blocking attempt and reports success with a boolean.
gotchas: Call Unlock only after a successful Lock, and do not unlock a mutex that is already unlocked.
Unlocking an unlocked mutex causes a fatal runtime error.

interview.question: What does sync.Once do?
interview.answer: Do runs its function only for the first call made on a particular Once value. Later calls return after the first function has finished.
interview.followUp: What happens if two goroutines call Do together? The mutex makes one run the function, while the other waits before returning.

interview.question: Why does Do use a mutex as well as an atomic flag?
interview.answer: The done flag is stored only after f returns. This ensures another caller cannot return before the initialization function finishes.
interview.followUp: Why not use only an atomic compare-and-swap? A losing caller could return while the winning caller was still running f.

interview.question: How can Do receive initialization arguments?
interview.answer: The function passed to Do has no arguments or return values. Use a function literal when initialization needs captured values.
interview.followUp: How can initialization report an error? sync.Once itself has no error result, so the function must store the error in shared state protected by the initialization pattern.

After Do returns, callers can safely observe initialization performed by f.
Already-completed calls use a fast path that checks the done state.

sync.RWMutex.summary: sync.RWMutex allows many readers or one writer to access shared data. A waiting writer prevents new readers from entering, which helps the writer eventually acquire the lock.
sync.RWMutex.explanation: An RWMutex protects shared data with either many simultaneous readers or one writer. A writer blocks new readers while it waits, so writers can eventually acquire the lock.

interview.question: What is the difference between RLock and Lock?
interview.answer: RLock permits several readers at once, while Lock permits only one writer and excludes readers. A writer waiting on active readers also prevents new readers from acquiring the lock.
interview.followUp: Can a reader upgrade its lock? No. The documentation says an RLock cannot be upgraded into a Lock, so release the read lock and use a separate design.

interview.question: What does RUnlock do?
interview.answer: RUnlock releases one read lock and does not release other readers' locks. It is a run-time error if the mutex is not read-locked when RUnlock is called.
interview.followUp: What happens if Unlock is called without a write lock? That is also a run-time error.

interview.question: How should an RWMutex be initialized and owned?
interview.answer: The zero value of RWMutex is ready for use and represents an unlocked mutex. After first use, the value must not be copied.
interview.followUp: Does a lock belong to the goroutine that acquired it? No. One goroutine may acquire it and another may release it.

keyPoints: Use RLock and RUnlock for shared read access. Use Lock and Unlock for exclusive write access.
You can declare an RWMutex without a constructor.
Each successful RLock needs one matching RUnlock.
A write lock waits when another writer or any reader currently holds the lock.
RLocker adapts read locking to the Locker interface by using RLock and RUnlock.

You cannot safely turn an existing read lock into a write lock.
You cannot turn a write lock into a read lock through the RWMutex API.
Keep the same RWMutex value after its first use; copy it before use only.

sync.WaitGroup.explanation: A WaitGroup tracks unfinished tasks with a counter. Add increases the counter, Done decreases it, and Wait blocks until the counter reaches zero. Go combines adding a task with starting a goroutine. A WaitGroup must not be copied after first use.

interview.question: What does a WaitGroup do?
interview.answer: A WaitGroup holds a task counter. Add increases it, Done decreases it, and Wait blocks until it is zero.
interview.followUp: When may a positive Add occur? If the counter is zero, it must occur before Wait; if the counter is already positive, it may occur at any time.

interview.question: How does WaitGroup.Go work?
interview.answer: Go adds one task and starts f in a new goroutine. When f returns normally or with runtime.Goexit, the task is removed.
interview.followUp: Can a task started by Go start another task? Yes, when the WaitGroup is not empty, the new Go call may happen at any time.

interview.question: How should tasks signal completion?
interview.answer: Done is equivalent to Add(-1). Its completion synchronizes before the return of a Wait call that it unblocks.
interview.followUp: What happens if a WaitGroup is reused too early? Wait can panic if it is reused before an earlier Wait has returned.

Done reduces the task counter by one.
Wait pauses the caller while unfinished tasks remain.
Go starts f in a new goroutine and records it as an unfinished task.
When no task is active, call Go before calling Wait.

Calling Done too many times, or using Add with an invalid negative result, causes a panic.
When reusing a WaitGroup, start the next task set only after the previous Wait returns.
The function passed to Go must not panic.

interview.question: What is a table-driven test?
interview.answer: A table-driven test keeps test cases in a slice, usually with fields for inputs and expected results. A loop applies one shared test body to every row, which avoids repeated test code.
interview.followUp: Why use a named subtest? Its name identifies the failing case, so the error message can stay short while the test output shows which row failed.

interview.question: What does t.Run add to table-driven tests?
interview.answer: Use t.Run with a name for each table row. Go reports each row as a separate subtest, so multiple failing cases can be shown independently.
interview.followUp: How can one subtest be selected? Use the -run flag with a slash-separated regular expression that matches the test and subtest names.

Worker pools.summary: A worker pool uses a fixed number of goroutines to process many tasks concurrently. A task queue feeds workers, and an optional result queue collects their results.
Worker pools.explanation: A worker pool uses a fixed group of goroutines that read tasks from a shared channel. The pool limits concurrent work, spreads tasks among workers, collects results when needed, and can stop cleanly when its context is cancelled.

interview.question: What problem does a worker pool solve?
interview.answer: A worker pool creates a limited set of worker goroutines and sends tasks to them through a shared queue. This avoids starting an unlimited number of goroutines and provides control over concurrency.
interview.followUp: What can happen if tasks arrive faster than workers finish? The queue can apply backpressure, so producers wait instead of allowing unbounded work to accumulate.

interview.question: How do you choose the number of workers?
interview.answer: The worker count should match the workload. CPU-heavy tasks usually need a count related to available CPU capacity, while I/O-heavy tasks can often use more workers because workers spend time waiting.
interview.followUp: How would you tune the count? Measure throughput, queue delay, resource use, and task latency under realistic load, then adjust the count.

interview.question: How should a worker pool shut down?
interview.answer: A clean shutdown stops new work, lets workers finish or cancel current work as designed, closes or drains the task path safely, and releases resources. Context-aware operation helps cancellation reach workers.
interview.followUp: Why is closing shared channels delicate? A sender must not send after the channel is closed, so ownership of closing and shutdown ordering must be clear.

keyPoints: Workers process similar tasks in parallel.
Reuse workers instead of creating one goroutine for every task.
A task channel sends work to available workers.
A result channel can carry completed results back to the caller.
The pool limits how many goroutines run concurrently.
The queue provides backpressure when producers submit work faster than workers finish it.
gotchas: Do not choose the worker count without considering the workload. CPU-bound and I/O-bound tasks may need different counts.
Workers must handle errors instead of silently ignoring failed tasks.
Stop the pool cleanly and release resources used by workers.
